rules.title: Rules of thumb
rules.r1: Every iPhone from XS / XR (2018) onward, all iPads with cellular from 2018+, and every Apple Watch Cellular — except units bought in mainland China, Hong Kong, or Macao.
rules.r2: Samsung Galaxy S20 and newer, Note 20 series, all foldables (Z Fold / Z Flip), the A54 / A55 / A56 / A57, and Galaxy Watch LTE from 3 onward.
rules.r3: Google Pixel 5 and newer, all Pixel Watch LTE, all iPads cellular, cellular Galaxy Tab S7+ and later, and modern 5G mobile hotspots (Nighthawk M5+, Solis 5G, GlocalMe).
rules.r4: Any phone from before 2018 (with rare exceptions), most Redmi / POCO, Samsung A/M/F series below A54, Wi-Fi-only tablets, non-cellular smartwatches, and every feature phone.
rules.footnoteHtml: Compiled from public specs and carrier lists (Apple, Vodafone UK, Klook, Cybernews, esim-now, mysimguide — August 2026). Regional variants sometimes differ; when in doubt, dial *#06# — if you see an EID line, your device has eSIM hardware.
faq.title: eSIM questions, answered
faq.q1: How do I check if my phone supports eSIM?
faq.a1Html: Search your brand and model above, or the model code printed in your phone’s settings. You can also dial *#06#: if an EID line appears, the device has eSIM hardware.
faq.a2Html: The EID (eUICC identifier) is a 32-digit number that identifies the eSIM chip inside your device. Only devices with eSIM hardware have one.
faq.q3: Why can the same model differ by region?
faq.a3Html: Manufacturers ship regional versions. Most iPhones sold in mainland China, Hong Kong and Macao use two physical SIMs instead of eSIM, while US iPhone 14 and later are eSIM-only. Check the exact model code.
faq.q4: Does my phone need to be unlocked?
faq.a4Html: Yes. A carrier-locked phone may refuse eSIM profiles from other providers even if it has eSIM hardware. Ask your carrier to unlock it before installing a new eSIM.
faq.q5: How do I install an Openline eSIM?
faq.a5Html: If your device is compatible and unlocked, buy a plan at openline.com and scan the QR code under Settings › Cellular (iPhone) or Settings › Connections › SIM manager (most Android phones).
nf.title: Page not found · Openline Check
nf.p: But your device might still support eSIM.
exp.carrierWatch: Cellular smartwatches get their eSIM through a carrier watch plan, set up from the paired phone’s companion app (Apple Watch app, Galaxy Wearable, Pixel Watch app). Phone or travel eSIM QR codes can’t be installed on the watch directly, so check that your carrier offers a plan for this watch.
exp.gpsOnly: This is the GPS-only version. It has no cellular radio, so it can’t use any eSIM. The GPS + Cellular version of the same watch has a different model number.
exp.cnHkMoDualNano: iPhones sold in mainland China, Hong Kong and Macao for this generation have two physical nano-SIM slots and no eSIM. Openline can’t install on these units. Check the model number under Settings › General › About.
exp.cnDualNano: The mainland China version of this phone uses two physical nano-SIM cards and has no eSIM. Models sold everywhere else support eSIM. Check the model number under Settings › General › About.
exp.cnLocalRules: The mainland China version supports eSIM, but Chinese carriers only activate eSIM in their stores with ID checks, and overseas eSIM profiles can’t be installed while you’re in mainland China. Outside China, travel eSIMs such as Openline install normally.
exp.esimOnlyUsJpCaGulf: Units sold in the United States, Canada, Japan, Mexico and the Gulf states have no SIM tray and work with eSIM only. Elsewhere the phone also has a nano-SIM tray, and mainland China units may lack eSIM. Openline works on every eSIM-capable version.
exp.noSimTray: This version has no physical SIM tray: every line, including Openline, is added as an eSIM. You can store several eSIMs and switch between them in Settings.
exp.iden: This device runs on Motorola’s iDEN network (Nextel / Boost push-to-talk), which was fully decommissioned by Sprint in June 2013. It cannot connect to any modern cellular network — eSIM or otherwise. Museum/collector item only.
exp.cdmaVerizon: This is a CDMA-only device built for Verizon’s legacy 2G/3G CDMA network, which was shut down on December 31, 2022. It has no SIM slot at all (physical or eSIM) — CDMA authenticates on the network via the device’s ESN/MEID, not a SIM. It cannot be used with Openline or any modern carrier.
exp.cdmaSprint: This is a CDMA device built for Sprint’s legacy network, which T-Mobile shut down permanently on May 31, 2022. Newer Sprint models added LTE/GSM but earlier ones are CDMA-only and cannot connect to any modern network — with or without eSIM.
exp.sunset: This device relies on 3G or older 4G networks that carriers have shut down (AT&T 3G ended February 2022, T-Mobile February 2022, Verizon December 2022, most European 3G by 2025). Even if it has a working SIM slot, there’s no network for it to connect to in most countries.
exp.windowsPhone: This runs Windows Phone (or Windows 10 Mobile), which Microsoft discontinued in 2019 — the Store, security patches, and most first-party services are all shut down. It has no eSIM hardware and virtually no modern app support. Unusable as a daily driver.
exp.kaios: This is a KaiOS feature phone. Almost no KaiOS device supports eSIM — they use a physical SIM (usually a nano-SIM) and are targeted at cheap 4G-only feature-phone markets like India (JioPhone) and Africa. Openline cannot install here.
exp.telematics: This is a vehicle telematics module (Tesla, BMW, Audi, etc.) with a factory-embedded eSIM soldered onto the car’s connectivity board. The eSIM is provisioned by the automaker at the factory and cannot be swapped for a user-installed profile like Openline. Not user-serviceable.
exp.satellite: This is a satellite/GPS communicator (Garmin inReach, SPOT, Zoleo, Iridium GO) that uses the Iridium or Globalstar satellite network — not GSM/LTE cellular. It cannot use an eSIM in the conventional sense; connectivity is tied to a proprietary subscription with the tracker’s manufacturer.
exp.medical: This is a medical alert or PERS (personal emergency response) device. Its cellular radio is locked to the service provider (Lively, Medical Guardian, Life Alert, Bay Alarm) and only works with their monitoring subscription. It cannot install third-party eSIMs.
exp.rugged: This is a Samsung Enterprise / Rugged (Galaxy XCover series) device intended for field workforces — warehouses, healthcare, hospitality. It supports eSIM but activation may go through your employer’s Samsung Knox MDM configuration. Openline installs like on any consumer phone if the device is unlocked.
exp.harmony: This device runs HarmonyOS (Huawei) with no Google Mobile Services. eSIM activation typically requires the Huawei EMUI/HarmonyOS carrier-services app; Openline profiles will provision via the QR code, but Google Wallet-based activations do not work. Devices sold in mainland China may additionally reject international eSIM profiles due to CN firmware restrictions.
exp.dualEsimOnly: This variant supports two eSIMs simultaneously but has no physical SIM tray. Openline works — you just cannot combine it with a nano-SIM. On some regional builds only one eSIM can be active at a time.
exp.euCarrier: Some European carrier-locked variants of this device shipped with eSIM disabled at the firmware level. Unlocked/global-open models support eSIM normally. Check with your original carrier if activation fails.
exp.usCarrier: This is a US-carrier-branded variant (AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon, Sprint) with locked firmware and often carrier-specific band support. eSIM may be disabled or restricted to the branding carrier’s profiles. Unlocked international units of the same model typically work with Openline; carrier-branded units may not.
exp.verizon: Verizon-branded units of this Pixel had eSIM disabled at launch on the Verizon network. Unlocked and non-Verizon carrier units support eSIM normally.
exp.googleFi: On this generation of Pixel, eSIM was only available through Google Fi in the US. Other carriers used physical SIM only. Global unlocked units support eSIM everywhere.
exp.usEsimOnly: On US-purchased units of this iPhone, Apple removed the physical SIM tray entirely — you must use an eSIM. Everywhere else, the phone has a physical SIM tray in addition to eSIM. Openline still works either way.
exp.cnOnly: This device ships with China-domestic firmware. eSIM support is present on paper but international profiles frequently fail to activate outside mainland China. If you plan to travel, verify eSIM activation with the seller before purchase.
exp.jpDomestic: Japanese carrier-branded phones (NTT DoCoMo, au, SoftBank, Rakuten) are usually band-locked to Japan’s frequency plan. eSIM hardware works in Japan; overseas activation depends on band overlap with local networks.
exp.regionLocked: This device’s eSIM activation is region-locked at the firmware level. It only accepts eSIM profiles from carriers in the country/region it was sold in.
exp.krOnly: This model is only sold in South Korea and uses KT/SKT/LGU+ carrier bands. eSIM hardware is present but activation abroad is unreliable.
exp.foldable: This is a foldable device — the eSIM slot is present but note that some foldable variants sold in China omit international eSIM support. Verify the model code matches the global SKU.
exp.hotspot: This is a portable Wi-Fi hotspot / MiFi router rather than a phone. It accepts an eSIM to share cellular data with your other devices. Openline provisions the same way as on a phone.
exp.simTrayOnly: This device has a cellular radio, but only accepts a physical nano-SIM or micro-SIM — there’s no eSIM chip. You can’t install Openline as an eSIM here; you’d need a physical SIM plan instead.
exp.wifiOnly: This variant is Wi-Fi only — no cellular modem. It cannot install any eSIM. Look for the LTE / 5G / Cellular version of the same model.
exp.ereader: This is an e-reader with a factory-embedded cellular modem tied to the manufacturer’s free-data plan (Amazon Whispernet, B&N nook, etc.). The eSIM/SIM is not user-provisionable — you can’t swap in an Openline profile.
exp.cellularEsimOnly: This variant has cellular connectivity via eSIM only — there’s no physical SIM tray on the device. Openline installs directly via QR code.
exp.unverifiedVariant: Our data links this model code to more than one product family. That usually means Apple/Samsung/Google reused an internal number across generations, or a regional SKU was renamed. Openline should still work, but if the model number on the box doesn’t match the device you’re looking at, double-check with the manufacturer before purchase.
exp.crossBrand: This model code also appears on a device from a different brand (Vivo/iQOO, Xiaomi/POCO, Nokia/HMD, Nubia/ZTE etc.). That’s usually a corporate sibling — the hardware is often identical, sometimes rebadged — but eSIM support and carrier certification can differ between the two brands. Verify against your unit’s actual retail packaging.
exp.modelUnverified: We don’t have an authoritative model/part number for this device — usually because it’s a wearable, vehicle telematics unit, hotspot, or accessory whose SKU isn’t publicly published. eSIM support is on the manufacturer’s spec sheet, but Openline can’t match a specific hardware code to guarantee compatibility. Verify with the maker before relying on it.
exp.ambiguous: The product name here is very short (“13”, “F7”, “M6”…) and easy to confuse with same-numbered models from other brands or generations. Check the brand and model code on your device to make sure this entry actually matches what you own.
exp.cnFirmware: This unit ships with China-domestic firmware. eSIM hardware is present, but the Chinese firmware often blocks activation of international eSIM profiles. If you plan to use Openline outside mainland China, verify with the seller that the firmware isn’t region-locked before purchase.
exp.regionExcluded: Units of this device sold in the following regions ship without eSIM hardware, so only the physical SIM tray works: {regions}. Everywhere else, eSIM is supported and Openline will activate normally. If you bought yours abroad or through a grey-market importer, check the model number against the manufacturer’s list.
